name: Cloud-Native Patterns

beginner.content:
Externalized Configuration Pattern

Externalized Configuration means keeping configuration values - database URLs, credentials, feature flags, timeouts - out of your compiled code and reading them instead from an external source: environment variables, config files, or a config server. This is the third factor of the well-known Twelve-Factor App methodology: "Store config in the environment."

Why It Matters


• No Rebuild Per Environment - The same compiled JAR runs in dev, staging, and production; only the config differs.
• Secrets Stay Out of Source Control - Credentials never get committed to Git.
• Change Without Redeploying - Some values (timeouts, flags) can be tuned without a full rebuild.

Spring Boot's application.yml + Profiles

Spring Boot's standard approach is application.yml (or .properties) combined with profiles - a "dev" profile and a "prod" profile can each override values like the database URL.
codeExamples:
# application.yml (base config, checked into Git - no secrets here)
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
server:
  port: ${SERVER_PORT:8080}

---
# application-prod.yml (activated with --spring.profiles.active=prod)
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}         # comes from an environment variable, not hardcoded
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}

expert.content:
Layered Config Resolution

Spring Boot resolves configuration from multiple sources in a defined precedence order (highest wins): command-line arguments > environment variables > profile-specific files (application-prod.yml) > the base application.yml > @PropertySource annotations > defaults in code.

Related Patterns

• Configuration Server Pattern - one way to implement Externalized Configuration centrally across MANY services, instead of each service reading its own local files.
• Distributed Configuration Pattern - goes a step further, propagating config CHANGES live to already-running instances, not just at startup.

This pattern (Externalized Configuration) is the foundational principle; the other two are specific mechanisms for implementing it at scale.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why not just hardcode the DB URL in the code?It would require a rebuild for every environment and risk leaking credentials into source control
Which Twelve-Factor App principle does this map to?Factor III - "Store config in the environment"
What resolves with the highest precedence in Spring Boot config?Command-line arguments, followed by environment variables, then profile-specific files, then the base application.yml
How does this differ from the Configuration Server pattern?Externalized Configuration is the general principle (config outside code); Configuration Server is one specific centralized mechanism for serving that config to many services

beginner.content:
Health Check Pattern

A Health Check is an endpoint a service exposes so external systems - load balancers, orchestrators like Kubernetes, monitoring tools - can ask "are you okay?" and get a simple, fast answer. Instances that report unhealthy get taken out of rotation automatically, before they cause customer-facing failures.

Spring Boot Actuator's /health Endpoint

Spring Boot Actuator ships a ready-made /actuator/health endpoint that aggregates the status of the app itself plus its dependencies (database, disk space, message brokers).
codeExamples:
# pom.xml dependency
# <dependency>
#   <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
#   <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
# </dependency>

# application.yml
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: always

expert.content:
Liveness vs Readiness Probes (Kubernetes)

Kubernetes distinguishes two different health questions, and conflating them is a classic production mistake:

ProbeQuestion It AnswersWhat Happens on Failure
LivenessIs the process stuck/deadlocked?Kubernetes kills and restarts the container
ReadinessIs the instance ready to receive traffic right now?Kubernetes stops routing traffic to it, but does NOT restart it

A service warming up a cache at startup should fail readiness (don't send it traffic yet) while still passing liveness (it's not stuck, just busy) - conflating the two would cause needless restart loops.
codeExamples:
# Kubernetes deployment snippet (illustrative YAML, not Java output)
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/liveness
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/readiness
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 5

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the difference between liveness and readiness probes?Liveness asks "should this be restarted?"; readiness asks "should this receive traffic right now?" - they can disagree (e.g. warming up)
Why is a health check important for load balancers?It lets the load balancer automatically stop routing traffic to unhealthy instances instead of serving errors to users
What does Spring Boot Actuator provide out of the box?A /actuator/health endpoint that aggregates the app's own status plus dependency health (DB, disk, message broker)

beginner.content:
Service Mesh Pattern

A Service Mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication concerns - retries, timeouts, load balancing, mutual TLS encryption, observability - outside your application code, typically via a sidecar proxy deployed alongside every service instance.

Why Not Just Put This Logic in the App?


• Every service would need to reimplement retry/timeout/TLS logic in every language it's written in.
• A service mesh centralizes it in the infrastructure layer instead, so application code stays focused on business logic.
• Real examples: Istio, whose data plane is built on the Envoy proxy, and Linkerd, which deliberately ships its own lightweight Rust micro-proxy instead of Envoy.

expert.content:
How It Works: Sidecar Proxies

Each service instance gets a sidecar proxy (e.g. Envoy) deployed in the same pod. All inbound and outbound traffic for that service is transparently routed through its sidecar, which enforces mesh-wide policies (mTLS, retries, circuit breaking) without the service's own code knowing anything about it. This is a direct application of the Sidecar Pattern at the networking layer - the mesh's "data plane" is made up of all these sidecars, coordinated by a "control plane" that pushes configuration to them.

   Service A            Service B
  +---------+          +---------+
  |  App A  |          |  App B  |
  +---------+          +---------+
  | Sidecar |<------->| Sidecar |   <- mTLS, retries, metrics happen here
  +---------+          +---------+
       ^                    ^
       |                    |
       +---- Control Plane -+   (pushes routing/security policy to every sidecar)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does a service mesh solve?It moves cross-cutting service-to-service communication concerns (retries, mTLS, observability) out of application code into a dedicated infrastructure layer
What is the "data plane" vs "control plane" in a mesh?The data plane is the set of sidecar proxies actually handling traffic; the control plane pushes configuration/policy down to those proxies
Name two real service mesh implementations.Istio (Envoy-based data plane) and Linkerd (its own Rust micro-proxy, not Envoy)

beginner.content:
Configuration Server Pattern

A Configuration Server is a dedicated centralized service that stores and serves configuration for ALL of an organization's other services, instead of each service keeping its own local config files. Spring Cloud Config Server is the standard Java/Spring implementation - it typically backs onto a Git repository as the source of truth for config.

Relationship to Externalized Configuration

Externalized Configuration is the general principle - "keep config outside code." A Configuration Server is one specific way to implement that principle centrally, which becomes valuable once you have dozens of services and copy-pasting config files everywhere no longer scales.
codeExamples:
# Config Server's application.yml
spring:
  cloud:
    config:
      server:
        git:
          uri: https://github.com/myorg/config-repo

# order-service's bootstrap.yml (client side) - illustrative, not deterministic Java output
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
  cloud:
    config:
      uri: http://config-server:8888
# order-service fetches order-service.yml from the config repo at startup

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why use a Config Server instead of local application.yml files per service?It centralizes config for many services in one auditable place (typically Git-backed), instead of scattering/duplicating files across every service's repo
What's the standard Java implementation of this pattern?Spring Cloud Config Server
Does a Config Server alone propagate live config changes to running instances?Not by itself - that's the job of the related Distributed Configuration pattern (e.g. paired with Spring Cloud Bus)

beginner.content:
Centralized Logging Pattern

In a system with many service instances (potentially auto-scaling up and down), logs scattered across individual machines are useless during an incident - you can't SSH into a container that no longer exists. Centralized Logging ships every instance's logs to one aggregated, searchable place instead.

The ELK/EFK Stack


• Filebeat/Fluentd - lightweight agents that read log files/streams and forward them.
• Logstash (or Fluentd in EFK) - parses/enriches log lines.
• Elasticsearch - stores and indexes logs for fast search.
• Kibana - the UI for searching and visualizing logs.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is per-machine logging insufficient in the cloud?Instances are ephemeral (auto-scaled, replaced on failure) - their local logs disappear with them, so aggregation elsewhere is required
What does the "L" in ELK stand for?Logstash - the component that parses and enriches incoming log data before indexing
Why attach structured fields (like orderId) via MDC instead of just free text?Structured fields become searchable/filterable in the log aggregation tool, instead of requiring fragile text parsing

beginner.content:
Distributed Tracing Pattern

When one user request fans out across five microservices, a single log file can't show you the whole picture. Distributed Tracing tags a request with a shared trace ID the moment it enters the system, and propagates that ID through every downstream call, so all the pieces can be reassembled into one timeline later.

Spring Cloud Sleuth + Zipkin/Jaeger

Spring Cloud Sleuth (or its successor, Micrometer Tracing) automatically injects trace IDs and span IDs into logs and outgoing HTTP/messaging calls. Zipkin or Jaeger then collect and visualize those traces.

expert.content:
Why This Matters for Latency Debugging

A trace is built from spans - one span per unit of work (an HTTP call, a DB query). Visualized as a waterfall/flame graph, spans immediately reveal WHICH service in a five-hop chain is actually responsible for a slow request, instead of guessing from disconnected logs.

traceId=8f3a1c
  Gateway         [====] 20ms
    OrderService    [========] 80ms
      PaymentService  [========================] 240ms  <- the actual bottleneck
      InventoryService[==] 15ms

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a trace ID?A unique identifier generated when a request enters the system, propagated through every downstream call so the full request path can be reconstructed
What is a span?One unit of work within a trace - e.g. one HTTP call or one DB query - with its own start/end time
Name two tools used to visualize distributed traces.Zipkin and Jaeger

beginner.content:
Auto Scaling Pattern

Auto Scaling automatically adds or removes running instances of a service based on real-time load, instead of provisioning for peak capacity 24/7 (wasteful) or fixed capacity (risks overload during spikes).

Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)

The HPA watches a metric (commonly CPU or memory utilization, or a custom metric like queue depth) and adjusts the number of pod replicas to keep it near a target.
codeExamples:
# HorizontalPodAutoscaler manifest (illustrative YAML, not Java output)
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: order-service-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: order-service
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does auto scaling solve?Avoids over-provisioning for peak load 24/7 while still handling traffic spikes, by dynamically adjusting instance count to real-time load
What metric does the Kubernetes HPA commonly scale on?CPU/memory utilization by default, or a custom metric like queue depth or request rate
Why does auto scaling depend on Graceful Shutdown working correctly?When scaling down, terminated instances must finish in-flight requests cleanly instead of dropping them - otherwise scale-down events cause user-facing errors

beginner.content:
Graceful Shutdown Pattern

When an instance is being terminated - during a deploy, a scale-down, or a node failure - Graceful Shutdown means it finishes any in-flight requests and cleans up resources (closes DB connections, flushes queues) before actually exiting, instead of being killed mid-request.

Spring Boot's Built-In Support

Spring Boot (2.3+) supports graceful shutdown out of the box - when it receives a termination signal, it stops accepting NEW requests but lets in-flight ones complete, up to a configurable timeout.
codeExamples:
# application.yml
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s
# On SIGTERM: Spring Boot stops accepting new connections immediately,
# but gives in-flight requests up to 20 seconds to finish before forcing exit.

expert.content:
Why This Matters During Deploys and Scaling

Without graceful shutdown, every rolling deploy or auto-scale-down event would abruptly cut off whatever requests happened to be in progress on the terminated instance, producing user-visible errors on a completely routine operation. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM first, waits for a configurable terminationGracePeriodSeconds, and only sends SIGKILL if the process hasn't exited by then - the app's shutdown logic must fit within that window.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What signal does Kubernetes send before forcefully killing a pod?SIGTERM first, giving the app a grace period, then SIGKILL if it hasn't exited
What happens to in-flight requests during graceful shutdown?The instance stops accepting NEW requests but is allowed to finish already-in-progress ones before exiting
Why does this matter especially with auto scaling?Scale-down events happen routinely under normal operation, so without graceful shutdown they'd regularly cause dropped requests

beginner.content:
Leader Election Pattern

Some tasks - a scheduled cleanup job, a cache-warming routine - must run on exactly one instance, even though a service runs many replicas for availability. Leader Election coordinates those replicas to agree on exactly one "leader" responsible for the task; if the leader dies, the remaining instances elect a new one.

Real Implementations


• Kubernetes Lease objects - a built-in primitive apps can use to coordinate leadership via the Kubernetes API.
• Apache ZooKeeper - a classic distributed coordination service, commonly used for leader election via ephemeral sequential znodes.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why not just always run a scheduled job on every instance?It would run duplicated N times (once per instance) instead of once - Leader Election ensures exactly one runs it
What happens when the current leader instance dies?Its lease/lock expires or is released, and another instance detects this and becomes the new leader
Name two real coordination mechanisms used for leader election.Kubernetes Lease objects and Apache ZooKeeper

beginner.content:
Distributed Configuration Pattern

Distributed Configuration is about propagating configuration changes consistently and in near real time to many ALREADY-RUNNING instances - not just reading config once at startup. This is the piece Externalized Configuration and Configuration Server don't fully solve on their own.

How the Three Related Patterns Differ


• Externalized Configuration - the general principle of keeping config outside compiled code (WHERE it lives).
• Configuration Server - one specific mechanism for centrally SERVING that config to many services, typically read once at startup.
• Distributed Configuration (this pattern) - specifically about PROPAGATING live CHANGES to instances that are already running, without a restart.

Spring Cloud Bus

Spring Cloud Bus links a Config Server to a lightweight message broker (RabbitMQ/Kafka); a single /actuator/busrefresh call broadcasts a "config changed" event to every connected service instance, which then re-reads its config live.
codeExamples:
# One HTTP call refreshes ALL connected instances' config live:
# POST http://config-server:8888/actuator/busrefresh
# (illustrative - actual effect is distributed and asynchronous, not deterministic Java output)

expert.content:
Alternative: A Watched Distributed Key-Value Store

Instead of a message-bus broadcast, some systems use a distributed key-value store like etcd, Consul, or ZooKeeper - services "watch" specific keys, and the store pushes a notification to every watcher the instant a value changes, without needing a separate broker in the mix.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does Distributed Configuration differ from just using a Config Server?A Config Server typically serves config once at startup; Distributed Configuration is specifically about pushing live CHANGES to already-running instances
What does Spring Cloud Bus add on top of Spring Cloud Config Server?A message-broker-backed broadcast mechanism (/actuator/busrefresh) that notifies all connected instances of a config change at once
Name a distributed key-value store alternative to a bus-based approach.etcd, Consul, or ZooKeeper - using their "watch" capability on specific keys

cheatNotes: Externalized Configuration - keep config OUT of compiled code (Twelve-Factor Factor III)
Health Check - /actuator/health tells load balancers/orchestrators if an instance is OK
Liveness probe = restart me?, Readiness probe = send me traffic?
Service Mesh - sidecar proxies (Envoy for Istio, a Rust proxy for Linkerd) handle retries/mTLS/observability outside app code
Configuration Server (Spring Cloud Config) - centrally SERVES config to many services
Centralized Logging (ELK/EFK) - aggregate logs since instances are ephemeral
Distributed Tracing - one traceId follows a request across every microservice hop
Auto Scaling (K8s HPA) - adjusts instance count to real-time load automatically
Graceful Shutdown - finish in-flight requests before exiting on SIGTERM
Leader Election - exactly one instance owns a task among many replicas
Distributed Configuration - propagates live config CHANGES to running instances, not just at startup
